cases.abstract: FlexGen targets batch inference when large language model weights and key-value caches exceed GPU memory. Offloading caches permits larger batches, while processing multiple GPU batches with each loaded layer amortizes weight transfers. A cost model and linear programming select tensor placement across GPU, CPU, and disk. Without CPU computation, an idealized analysis bounds asymptotic weight I/O within twice the optimum. In dummy-weight OPT-175B benchmarks with 512-token prompts and 32 generated tokens, FlexGen achieves 0.69 tokens/s uncompressed, versus 0.01 for uncompressed Accelerate and DeepSpeed, on one 16-GB T4 with 208-GB CPU memory and a 1.5-TB SSD. Four-bit weight and cache compression without retraining or calibration raises throughput to 1.12 tokens/s by fitting tensors in host memory and avoiding disk transfers. Separate real-weight Lambada and WikiText evaluations show small quality changes, including with sparse value-cache access, but compression can slow models fitting GPU memory. Four-GPU offloading yields super-linear decoding scaling but sublinear overall scaling for 32-token generation. Completing seven HELM sub-scenarios with OPT-IML-30B in 21 hours, including overhead, establishes an end-to-end batch use case beyond synthetic throughput tests. The throughput gains suit workloads accepting long completion times and depend on host-memory capacity and storage bandwidth.
cases.notes: Sections 4 and 6.1 connect cache offloading to batch size and weight reuse to amortized I/O. Table 2 tests throughput, not low-latency serving; compression avoids disk I/O under Table 15's host-memory placement. Table 5 separately tests real-weight quality, so dummy-weight speed does not establish accuracy preservation. HELM supplies the end-to-end check. Retained the idealized weight-I/O bound, compression slowdowns, and decoding/overall scaling distinction. No causal attribution to each component or cross-GPU Petals superiority is claimed.

cases.abstract: Neural ODEs replace discrete hidden-state updates with neural-network dynamics integrated by a numerical solver. Adjoint training reconstructs states alongside gradients in a reverse-time augmented ODE, avoiding storage of intermediate solver operations and making memory independent of the number of function evaluations. Solver tolerances trade precision for computation. On MNIST, 0.42% test error with 0.22 million parameters, versus a residual network's 0.41% with 0.60 million, supports comparable classification with fewer parameters rather than improved accuracy. For dynamics uniformly Lipschitz in state and continuous in time, the instantaneous change-of-variables theorem expresses log-density evolution through a Jacobian trace rather than a determinant. Trace additivity permits continuous normalizing flows with density-update cost linear in hidden units per function evaluation; two-dimensional experiments illustrate density fitting and reversible sampling. A latent ODE uses shared continuous dynamics to evaluate irregularly observed trajectories at arbitrary times and can jointly model observation times through a Poisson likelihood. On synthetic noisy spirals with 30 of 100 observations, RMSE is 0.1642 versus 0.3937 for an RNN across 100 prediction times extending beyond training observations, supporting sparse-observation prediction in this setting. Reverse-time reconstruction can introduce numerical error; checkpointing mitigates it by storing intermediate states.
cases.notes: Sections 2-3 support trainable continuous dynamics: reverse-time state reconstruction removes the need to retain solver operations, while Table 1 shows comparable MNIST error with fewer parameters, not accuracy superiority. Section 4's trace additivity explains the density-modeling co-contribution; linear cost is per evaluation, not total solver runtime. Section 5 and Table 2 connect arbitrary-time trajectories to sparse synthetic-spiral prediction. Flow comparisons use different optimizers and iteration budgets, so no matched-budget advantage is inferred. Checkpointing retains states and changes the memory trade-off; garbled software names and tolerances remain omitted.
